notes.definition: Decomposition (decay) is the breakdown of dead organisms and waste by microorganisms such as bacteria and fungi. Its rate depends on temperature, the amount of water and the availability of oxygen.
explanation: Decay is carried out mainly by microorganisms: bacteria and fungi. They secrete enzymes onto dead material, which digest large insoluble molecules into small soluble ones. The microorganisms absorb these products and use them for respiration and growth. In doing so they return carbon dioxide to the atmosphere and mineral ions to the soil. Because decay depends on enzymes and on living microorganisms, any factor that affects enzyme activity or the growth and respiration of microorganisms affects the rate of decay.

Temperature: decay is faster in warm conditions because the enzymes of the decomposers work faster and the microorganisms grow and reproduce more quickly. At low temperatures decay is very slow (this is why fridges and freezers slow food spoilage). Above the optimum, enzymes begin to denature and the microorganisms may be killed, so decay slows or stops (this is why cooking and canning preserve food). Most decomposers work best at around 25 to 45 °C.

Water: decomposers need water to grow and reproduce. Their enzymes digest food in solution, and the soluble products are absorbed in solution. Dry material decays very slowly, which is why drying is used to preserve foods such as pasta, raisins and dried fish. Oxygen: most decomposers respire aerobically, so a good supply of oxygen speeds up decay. In waterlogged or compacted conditions with little oxygen, decay is slower. Anaerobic decay (without oxygen) by some bacteria produces methane gas.

Gardeners and farmers try to provide the optimum conditions for rapid decay of waste biological material. A compost heap is built from layers of garden and kitchen waste. It is kept moist, has gaps or holes so air can reach the microorganisms, and is turned regularly to add oxygen. Respiration of the microorganisms releases heat, keeping the heap warm, and the heap may be insulated or placed in the sun. Cutting material into small pieces increases the surface area for microorganisms to act on. The compost produced is used as a natural fertiliser for growing garden plants or crops, because it returns mineral ions to the soil.

Anaerobic decay produces methane gas. Biogas generators use this to produce methane as a fuel. Organic waste such as animal manure, food waste or plant material is put into a sealed tank (digester) with no oxygen, kept warm (about 30 to 40 °C). Anaerobic bacteria break the waste down, producing biogas, which is mainly methane with some carbon dioxide. Biogas can be burned for cooking, heating or generating electricity, and the remaining digested material can be used as a fertiliser. Biogas is a renewable fuel, and generators are used on farms, in sewage works and in many homes in rural areas of countries such as India and China.

Required practical 10 investigates the effect of temperature on the rate of decay of fresh milk by measuring pH change. Milk contains fat. The enzyme lipase breaks fat down into fatty acids and glycerol. The fatty acids lower the pH. In the experiment, milk is mixed with sodium carbonate solution (making it alkaline) and phenolphthalein indicator, which is pink in alkaline solutions and becomes colourless when the pH falls below about 8.3. The time for the pink colour to disappear is measured at different temperatures. A rate can be calculated as rate = 1000 ÷ time (in s). The rate increases with temperature up to an optimum (often around 35 to 45 °C) and then decreases as the lipase is denatured.
keyFacts: Decay is carried out by microorganisms (bacteria and fungi), which secrete enzymes to digest dead material.
Warm conditions speed up decay (faster enzyme activity); very high temperatures denature enzymes and slow or stop decay.
Moist conditions speed up decay: microorganisms need water, and digestion and absorption happen in solution.
Oxygen speeds up decay because most decomposers respire aerobically.
Gardeners make compost with warm, moist, aerated conditions; compost is a natural fertiliser.
Biogas generators use anaerobic decay of organic waste to produce methane as a fuel.
Required practical 10: lipase digests fat in milk to fatty acids, lowering the pH; phenolphthalein turns from pink to colourless.
Rate of decay can be calculated as 1000 ÷ time taken (s), or as change in mass or pH ÷ time.

keyTerms.definition: The breakdown of dead organisms and waste by microorganisms such as bacteria and fungi.
A microorganism (bacterium or fungus) that breaks down dead material by secreting enzymes and absorbing the products.
Decayed organic matter produced from garden and kitchen waste, used as a natural fertiliser.
Decay by microorganisms in the absence of oxygen, which produces methane gas.
A fuel gas made by anaerobic decay of organic waste, mainly methane with some carbon dioxide.
A sealed tank (digester) in which anaerobic bacteria break down organic waste to produce methane gas as a fuel.
An enzyme that breaks down lipids (fats) into fatty acids and glycerol.
An indicator that is pink in alkaline solutions and colourless when the pH falls below about 8.3.

equations.name: Rate from time taken
equations.units: s⁻¹ (when t is in seconds; the 1000 just makes the numbers easier to plot)

equations.name: Rate of change
equations.formula: rate of decay = change in quantity ÷ time taken
equations.units: for example g/day or pH units per minute

workedExamples.title: Calculating rate from time taken (required practical 10)
workedExamples.question: At 30 °C, a milk, lipase and phenolphthalein mixture took 250 s to turn colourless. Calculate the rate using rate = 1000 ÷ time.

workedExamples.title: Calculating rate of mass loss in compost
workedExamples.question: A bag of grass cuttings had a mass of 5.0 kg. After 8 weeks in a compost bin its mass was 2.6 kg. Calculate the mean rate of decay in kg per week.

workedExamples.title: Comparing rates at two temperatures
workedExamples.question: The milk mixture took 300 s to change colour at 20 °C and 120 s at 40 °C. Calculate how many times faster the rate is at 40 °C.
steps: Lipase molecules and substrate collide more often at the higher temperature.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the hotter it is, the faster decay always happens.
misconceptions.right: In fact decay speeds up only up to an optimum temperature; above it the decomposers' enzymes denature and the microorganisms may die, so decay slows down.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often say cold temperatures denature enzymes.
misconceptions.right: In fact low temperatures make enzymes work slowly (less kinetic energy, fewer collisions) but do not denature them; only high temperatures denature enzymes.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think decay stops completely without oxygen.
misconceptions.right: In fact anaerobic decay still happens, more slowly, and produces methane. This is the basis of biogas generators.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the pH rises in the milk practical because the milk goes off.
misconceptions.right: In fact lipase breaks fat into fatty acids, which lower the pH; the phenolphthalein turns colourless as the solution becomes less alkaline.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a longer time to change colour means a faster rate.
misconceptions.right: In fact rate is inversely related to time: rate = 1000 ÷ time, so a longer time means a slower rate.

realWorld: Local councils collect garden and food waste for industrial composting, producing compost that farmers and gardeners use as a natural fertiliser.
Many farms and sewage works use anaerobic digesters to turn manure and sewage into biogas, which generates electricity and heat.
Food preservation methods (refrigeration, freezing, drying, vacuum packing and canning) work by removing the warmth, water or oxygen that decomposers need.
separateOnlyContent: This whole subtopic is for separate Biology (8461) only and is not in Combined Science Trilogy.
How temperature, water and availability of oxygen affect the rate of decay of biological material.
Gardeners and farmers provide optimum conditions for rapid decay; compost is used as a natural fertiliser.
Anaerobic decay produces methane; biogas generators produce methane as a fuel.
Calculating rate changes in decay and translating between numerical and graphical data.
Required practical 10: effect of temperature on the rate of decay of fresh milk by measuring pH change.
examTips: When explaining why decay is faster in warm, moist, aerobic conditions, link each factor to the microorganisms: temperature to enzyme activity, water to growth and digestion in solution, oxygen to aerobic respiration.
In required practical 10, remember the chemistry: lipase converts fats into fatty acids and glycerol; the fatty acids lower pH; phenolphthalein goes from pink to colourless.
Use rate = 1000 ÷ time when the question asks; always show the division and give units if asked (s⁻¹).
When describing a graph of rate against temperature, give the optimum and describe the rise and fall with values, then explain using collisions and denaturing.
For biogas questions, state that anaerobic decay produces methane and that the digester must be sealed (no oxygen) and kept warm.
summary: Decay is the breakdown of dead material by bacteria and fungi using enzymes.
Decay is faster when warm (up to an optimum), moist and with oxygen.
Compost heaps are kept warm, moist and aerated; compost is a natural fertiliser.
Anaerobic decay produces methane; biogas generators use this as a fuel.
Required practical 10: lipase lowers the pH of milk; time for phenolphthalein to turn colourless measures rate.
Rate = 1000 ÷ time, or change in quantity ÷ time.

flashcards.back: Temperature, water (moisture) and availability of oxygen.

flashcards.back: Decomposer enzymes work faster and microorganisms grow and reproduce faster (up to an optimum).

flashcards.front: Why does water speed up decay?
flashcards.back: Microorganisms need water to grow; enzymes digest food in solution and products are absorbed in solution.

flashcards.front: Why does oxygen speed up decay?
What gas does anaerobic decay produce?

flashcards.back: A sealed tank where anaerobic bacteria break down organic waste to produce methane gas as a fuel.

flashcards.front: Why are compost heaps turned regularly?
flashcards.back: To add oxygen for aerobic respiration of the decomposers.
As a natural fertiliser for garden plants or crops.

flashcards.front: In RP10, what does lipase do to milk fat?

questions.question: Which gas is produced by anaerobic decay?
markScheme: 1 mark: methane
questions.explanation: Anaerobic bacteria break down organic matter without oxygen and release methane. This is the gas collected in biogas generators.

questions.question: Which set of conditions gives the fastest decay of garden waste?
markScheme: 1 mark: warm, moist, plenty of oxygen
questions.explanation: Decomposers need warmth for their enzymes, water to grow and digest food, and oxygen for aerobic respiration. Each other option lacks at least one of these.

questions.question: Which two groups of microorganisms are the main decomposers?
markScheme: 1 mark: bacteria and fungi
questions.explanation: Bacteria and fungi secrete enzymes to digest dead material. Viruses cannot feed or decompose material; algae are producers.

questions.question: What is compost used for by gardeners and farmers?
markScheme: 1 mark: as a natural fertiliser
questions.explanation: Compost returns mineral ions to the soil, so it acts as a natural fertiliser. Methane fuel comes from anaerobic biogas generators, not from aerobic compost.

questions.question:
A student investigated the effect of temperature on the rate of decay of milk.
The student added lipase to milk mixed with sodium carbonate solution and phenolphthalein indicator.
Why does the pH of the milk fall when lipase is added?
options: Lipase breaks down protein into amino acids
Lipase breaks down fat into fatty acids and glycerol
Lipase breaks down lactose into glucose
markScheme: 1 mark: lipase breaks down fat into fatty acids and glycerol
questions.explanation: Lipase digests lipids. The fatty acids produced are acidic, so the pH falls. Proteases digest protein, and lipase does not act on sugars.

questions.question:
A student added lipase to milk mixed with sodium carbonate solution and phenolphthalein indicator.
Which colour change shows that the pH has fallen enough?
markScheme: 1 mark: pink to colourless
questions.explanation: Phenolphthalein is pink in alkaline solution and turns colourless below about pH 8.3. Blue-black is the iodine test for starch.

questions.question: Why must a biogas generator be sealed?
options: To keep oxygen out so anaerobic bacteria produce methane
To let carbon dioxide in for the bacteria
To stop the waste from drying out only
markScheme: 1 mark: to keep oxygen out so anaerobic bacteria produce methane
questions.explanation: Methane is produced by anaerobic decay, so oxygen must be excluded. Sealing also lets the gas be collected. The digester is kept warm, not cold.

questions.question:
A student added lipase to milk mixed with sodium carbonate solution and phenolphthalein indicator. The student timed how long the mixture took to change colour at three temperatures.
Table 1 shows the results.
Which explanation for the result at 70 °C is correct?

headers: Time to change colour in s

options: At 70 °C the fat in the milk has evaporated
At 70 °C the lipase is denatured, so fewer active sites can bind to fat
markScheme: 1 mark: at 70 °C the lipase is denatured, so fewer active sites can bind to fat
questions.explanation: High temperatures change the shape of the active site, so the enzyme no longer fits its substrate. Low temperatures slow enzymes but do not denature them.

options: So that both solutions reach the bath temperature before the reaction starts
To allow the lipase to digest itself
To make the milk more acidic before starting
markScheme: 1 mark: so that both solutions reach the bath temperature before the reaction starts
questions.explanation: If the solutions were mixed at room temperature, the reaction would start at the wrong temperature, making the results invalid.

questions.question: Why does drying food (for example raisins or pasta) help to preserve it?
options: Microorganisms need water to grow and digest food
markScheme: 1 mark: microorganisms need water to grow and digest food
questions.explanation: Without water, decomposers cannot grow or reproduce, and their enzymes cannot digest food in solution, so decay is very slow.

questions.question: Name three factors that affect the rate of decay of biological material.
markScheme: 1 mark: temperature
1 mark: water (moisture)
1 mark: availability of oxygen
questions.explanation: These are the three factors named in the AQA specification. Each affects the growth or enzyme activity of decomposers.

questions.question: Name the main gas found in biogas.
markScheme: 1 mark: methane
questions.explanation: Biogas is mainly methane, with some carbon dioxide.

questions.question: Explain why decay is faster at 30 °C than at 5 °C.
markScheme: 1 mark: enzymes of the decomposers work faster / more collisions between enzymes and substrate
1 mark: microorganisms grow and reproduce faster / respire faster
questions.explanation: At higher temperatures (below the optimum) molecules have more kinetic energy, so enzyme-substrate collisions are more frequent and decomposers multiply faster.

questions.question: Explain why gardeners turn their compost heaps regularly.
markScheme: 1 mark: turning adds air / oxygen to the heap
1 mark: so decomposers can respire aerobically, and decay is faster
questions.explanation: Most decomposers in compost respire aerobically. Without turning, the centre of the heap becomes short of oxygen and decay slows.

questions.question: Give two uses of the biogas produced by a biogas generator.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any two from: cooking; heating (homes or water); generating electricity; lighting; fuel for vehicles
questions.explanation: Biogas is a fuel, so it is burned to release energy for heating, cooking or driving generators.

questions.question: A compost heap becomes hot in the centre, reaching 60 °C. Explain why the heap becomes hot and why decay may slow down if the temperature continues to rise.
markScheme: 1 mark: respiration by the microorganisms transfers energy as heat
1 mark: the heap insulates itself so heat builds up
1 mark: above the optimum the decomposers' enzymes denature / microorganisms are killed, so decay slows
questions.explanation: Respiration is exothermic. Warmth speeds decay up to a point, but too much heat denatures enzymes.

questions.question:
A student added lipase to milk mixed with sodium carbonate solution and phenolphthalein indicator. The student timed how long it took for the pink colour to disappear.
Suggest why it is difficult to judge the end point precisely, and suggest how the method could be improved.
markScheme: 1 mark: the colour change from pink to colourless is gradual / judging it is subjective
1 mark: so different times may be recorded for the same end point
1 mark: improvement: use a pH probe or data logger, or compare against a standard colour / view against a white background, with the same person judging each time
questions.explanation: A gradual colour change introduces human error. A pH meter gives an objective reading, or a reference tube can define the end point consistently.

questions.question:
A student investigated the effect of temperature on the rate of decay of milk.
Name the enzyme the student added to the milk.
markScheme: 1 mark: lipase
questions.explanation: Lipase breaks down the fat in milk into fatty acids and glycerol.

questions.question:
In an investigation into the decay of milk, a mixture took 250 s to turn colourless.
Calculate the rate of reaction.
Use the equation: rate = 1000 ÷ time
questions.explanation: Rate = 1000 ÷ 250 = 4 s⁻¹. A shorter time would give a larger rate.

questions.question:
A student timed how long a mixture of milk and lipase took to turn colourless at 25 °C.
Table 1 shows the results.
Calculate the mean time, then calculate the rate of reaction.
Use the equation: rate = 1000 ÷ mean time
Give your answer to 3 significant figures.

headers: Time to turn colourless in s

questions.explanation: Mean time = 570 ÷ 3 = 190 s. Rate = 1000 ÷ 190 = 5.263..., which is 5.26 to 3 significant figures.

questions.question:
A gardener measured the mass of a bag of grass cuttings as it composted.
Table 1 shows the results.
Calculate the mean rate of decay over the 8 weeks.

headers: Mass of grass cuttings in kg

markScheme: 1 mark: 2.4 ÷ 8 = 0.3 kg/week
questions.explanation: Use the first and last values in Table 1. Rate = change in mass ÷ time = (5.0 − 2.6) ÷ 8 = 2.4 ÷ 8 = 0.3 kg per week. Dividing the final mass by time (2.6 ÷ 8) is a common error.

A student used a pH probe to measure the pH of a mixture of milk and lipase.
Figure 1 shows the results.
Calculate the mean rate of pH change over the 12 minutes.

questions.question:
A student timed how long a mixture of milk and lipase took to change colour at two temperatures.
Table 1 shows the results.
Calculate how many times faster the rate is at 40 °C than at 20 °C.
Use the equation: rate = 1000 ÷ time

headers: Time to change colour in s

questions.explanation: Rates are 3.33 and 8.33 s⁻¹; their ratio is 2.5. You can check by dividing the times the other way round: 300 ÷ 120 = 2.5. Dividing 120 by 300 (0.4) gives the wrong way round.

questions.question:
A biogas generator produces 2.5 m³ of biogas per day. The biogas is 60% methane by volume.
Calculate the volume of methane produced in one week.
markScheme: 1 mark: methane per day = 2.5 × 0.60 = 1.5 m³
1 mark: per week = 1.5 × 7 = 10.5 m³
questions.explanation: 60% of 2.5 m³ is 1.5 m³ per day; over 7 days that is 10.5 m³. Forgetting the 60% gives 17.5 m³.

questions.question:
A student put leaves in a mesh bag and left the bag in leaf litter for 6 weeks.
Table 1 shows the results.
Calculate the percentage of the original mass that decayed.
questions.explanation: Mass lost = 180 g, which is 180 ÷ 500 × 100 = 36% of the original. Dividing 320 by 500 gives 64%, the mass remaining, not the mass decayed.

questions.question:
Describe a method to investigate the effect of temperature on the rate of decay of fresh milk.
You should use lipase, sodium carbonate solution and phenolphthalein indicator.
markScheme: Indicative content: measure a fixed volume of milk (for example 5 cm³) into a test tube; add a fixed volume of sodium carbonate solution (for example 7 cm³) to make it alkaline; add a few drops (for example 5) of phenolphthalein so the solution is pink; put a fixed volume of lipase solution (for example 1 cm³) in a separate tube; place both tubes in a water bath at a set temperature (for example 20 °C) and leave until they reach that temperature, checking with a thermometer; add the lipase to the milk, stir and start a stopwatch; stop the stopwatch when the pink colour disappears; repeat at other temperatures (for example 30, 40, 50, 60 °C); repeat each temperature three times and calculate a mean; calculate rate = 1000 ÷ time; keep volumes and concentrations the same.

Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a detailed, logically ordered method with correct use of all reagents, equilibration in the water bath, timing to the colour change, a range of temperatures, repeats and control variables.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a method that would work but with some omissions, for example no equilibration or no repeats.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple steps, for example 'mix milk and lipase at different temperatures and time it'.
questions.explanation: The key steps are: make alkaline milk with indicator, bring both solutions to temperature separately, mix and time the colour change, repeat across a range of temperatures, and calculate rate.

questions.question:
A farmer wants to deal with large amounts of cow manure. One option is to compost it in open heaps. Another is to put it in a biogas generator.
Compare the two methods, explaining the conditions each needs and the products made.
markScheme: Indicative content: composting: aerobic decay by bacteria and fungi; needs oxygen (turned regularly, air gaps), moisture, warmth; heat from respiration keeps it warm; produces compost used as natural fertiliser; releases carbon dioxide; open heaps may release some methane where oxygen is lacking. Biogas generator: anaerobic decay in a sealed tank with no oxygen; kept warm (about 30 to 40 °C) for the bacteria's enzymes; needs a regular supply of waste and must be maintained; produces biogas (mainly methane) used as a fuel for heating, cooking or electricity; the digested slurry is also used as fertiliser; burning methane releases carbon dioxide but it is a renewable fuel and replaces fossil fuels; methane is captured rather than escaping as a greenhouse gas; higher set-up cost than composting.

Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a clear comparison covering conditions (oxygen versus no oxygen, warmth, moisture) and products (compost versus methane fuel plus fertiliser), with explanation of why each condition is needed and a reasoned point about the benefits of each.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): describes conditions and products for both methods with limited explanation or comparison.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements about one or both methods.
questions.explanation: The central contrast is aerobic (compost) versus anaerobic (biogas). Strong answers explain why each condition is needed and note that both produce a fertiliser but only the generator makes a fuel.

questions.question: Explain how a gardener can provide the best conditions for rapid decay in a compost bin.
markScheme: Indicative content: keep the compost moist (add water if dry) because decomposers need water to grow and digest food; ensure oxygen by turning the heap or having air holes, as decomposers respire aerobically; keep it warm (place in the sun, insulate, use a lid or bin) because enzymes work faster; heat from respiration of microorganisms warms the heap; shred waste into small pieces to increase surface area for microorganisms; mix green and brown materials; do not let it become waterlogged, which reduces oxygen.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): describes how to provide at least two of warmth, moisture and oxygen, with a correct explanation for each.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): lists one or two conditions without explanation.
questions.explanation: Link each action to the decomposers' needs: warmth for enzymes, water for growth and digestion, oxygen for aerobic respiration.
